text: Lineage isn't bookkeeping for its own sake. Beyond 'it's good practice,' this lesson covers four concrete business reasons organizations invest in lineage, and what specifically breaks, in practical terms, when it doesn't exist or isn't trusted.

Trust first: when a number on a report looks wrong, the first question is always where did this actually come from. Without lineage the honest answer is often nobody fully knows — the report was built by someone who left, against a pipeline nobody documented. Impact analysis second: before changing a column name, a data type, or a transformation rule, lineage tells you exactly what else depends on it — this column feeds these six downstream tables and these three reports.

Root cause analysis: when a number is wrong, lineage lets you walk backward from the broken report to the exact hop where things diverged, instead of re-checking every system from scratch — a missing row might trace back to one filter added two transformations upstream. Audit and regulation: financial services, healthcare, and insurance must demonstrate exactly how a reported figure was calculated, from source to final number, for audit purposes.

Picture a quarterly revenue number that drops unexpectedly. Without lineage, three different people independently start checking three different systems, duplicating effort, because nobody has a map of which systems actually feed that number. The fix, once found, might be as small as one incorrectly-joined table — but finding it took days instead of minutes. With lineage in place, the team instead opens the record for that figure, sees every hop, and checks each one in order — mechanical instead of exploratory.

The Metadata Management course closed on giving every concept one definition and one home, rather than scattering it across spreadsheets that never agree. Lineage extends that idea from identity to movement — once a concept has one definition and one home, lineage proves every report pulling that concept is pulling it from that home, correctly, through every hop in between, rather than silently drifting onto a stale copy somewhere else.
Next up: business lineage versus technical lineage — the difference between a readable summary built for stakeholders and the detailed map engineers actually use to debug a broken column.
